title: Social Contract Theory Applied to Evaluating AI Deception: When Do Models Consider Deception Permissible?
original_idea: Design scenarios with varying social contract framings: deception in adversarial negotiation, deception of a trusted overseer, deception to prevent harm. Measure deception rates across framings. Assess whether models' stated justifications align with philosophical deception taxonomies.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: models have domain-specific deception norms -> adversaries exploit permissible-deception framings -> higher deception elicitation rates. The mechanism is plausible but the gap is whether the finding would be actionable for safety -- it characterizes a vulnerability but the mitigation path is unclear.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Scenario design and behavioral measurement via prompting is accessible. Comparing model responses to philosophical taxonomies requires some reading but no advanced ML skills. A beginner with guidance could construct the scenarios and run the measurements using API calls.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable: deception rate comparison across a small set of social contract framings on one model. Clear methodology (prompt model with scenarios, measure deception rate), few dependencies. The philosophical taxonomy comparison can be a second step.

novelty.reasoning: Research on LLMs in moral dilemmas exists ('When Ethics and Payoffs Diverge: LLM Agents in Morally Charged Social Dilemmas' arXiv:2505.19212, 2025), and 'Artificial Leviathan' (arXiv:2406.14373) explores social contract theory with LLM agents. AI-LIEDAR (arXiv:2409.09013) examines the trade-off between utility and truthfulness. However, the specific experimental design — systematically varying social contract framings (adversarial negotiation, trusted overseer, harm prevention) and measuring deception rates across framings, then mapping to philosophical deception taxonomies — appears novel. Existing work does not use social contract theory as a structured framework for understanding when models treat deception as permissible. The accessible methodology (prompt-based behavioral measurement) and clear first deliverable strengthen this idea.
